---
title: "Tracking Student Progress with OKRs"
description: "How we set, track, and review termly Objectives and Key Results for research students, and how we run the record-keeping through GitHub."
categories: [Project Management, OKRs]
---

## Why OKRs for a research group

Standard project management assumes you can specify the work up front and then execute against that 
specification. That assumption may hold for construction or manufacturing, but it usually doesn't 
work for research. In research, the deliverable itself is often unknown and the plan is expected to 
change as results come in.

Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) were built for a similar kind of uncertainty in fast-moving 
product teams. The idea is simple. Fix an ambitious direction, then let the tactics underneath it 
get rewritten on a regular, short cycle. That fits a research group well. A multi-year thesis 
timeline stays mostly fixed. What happens inside any given term should not.

## Three layers, three timescales

| Layer | Timescale | How often it changes | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Milestone map | Multi-year | Rarely | A document per student, updated as needed |
| Term OKRs | One term | Every term | The template below |
| Execution | Weekly | Constantly | Weekly check-ins and a task board |

The OKRs are the translation step between the two ends. They take a fixed multi-year milestone 
and ask what an honest, ambitious version of progress looks like over the next 4-month semester. 
Nobody replans the whole degree every term. Everybody replans the next term, every term.

## How the OKRs themselves work

**Objective.** One sentence, qualitative, ambitious. A direction worth pushing toward, not a 
checklist item.

**Key Results.** Two to four measurable outcomes that would only be true if the Objective actually 
happened. Each gets scored from 0.0 to 1.0 at the end of the term rather than marked simply done or 
not done.

**Scoring convention.** An average around 0.7 across a student's Key Results counts as a good term. 
Landing at 1.0 across the board usually means the Key Results were set too conservatively, not that 
the term went perfectly. This matters because it changes what people are willing to write down at 
the start of the term. If hitting 100% is the expectation, everyone writes safe targets. Evaluating 
on a curve that rewards ambition gets the honest version onto the page instead.

## The term cycle

1. **Week 1.** Supervisor and student set the term's Objective and Key Results together, in a short 
one-on-one conversation. Prior to this meeting, the student is expected to have done some preliminary
brainstorming and should come prepared with ideas for the term's direction. A group-level Objective 
for the term as a whole is set separately by the supervisor and shared with the group.
2. **Ongoing.** Weekly check-ins and a shared task board carry the week-to-week detail. There is no 
need to touch the OKR document itself between term start and the mid-term check.
3. **Mid-term.** A short confidence check per student. On track, at risk, or off track, with one line 
explaining why. This is also a natural point to notice whether the whole system is being used or 
quietly going stale.
4. **End of term.** The student self-scores each Key Result and writes a short reflection before the 
review meeting, then discusses it with the supervisor. Anything scored low but still relevant carries 
forward into the next term's Key Results. Anything low but no longer the right target is simply 
dropped, with no penalty for a term's plan turning out to be wrong.

## Template

### Group-level OKR (one per term)

```
Objective:

KR1:
KR2:
KR3:
```

### Individual OKR sheet (one per student, per term)

```
Objective:

KR1:
KR2:
KR3:
KR4 (optional):

Mid-term confidence check:
  Status: [on track / at risk / off track]
  Why (one line):

End of term:
  KR1 score (0.0-1.0):
  KR2 score:
  KR3 score:
  KR4 score:
  Reflection (2-3 sentences):
  Carry forward into next term:
```

### Objective examples by stage

These are starting points, not a script. The right Objective for a given student depends on where 
they actually are.

**Early stage**, building competence, no independent results yet.
Objective: build independent command of the core tool or method and produce a first credible result.
Key results: complete the core tutorial set unassisted, reproduce a known benchmark within a stated 
error tolerance, present a first talk on the result.

**Mid stage**, has a working method, needs to convert it into output.
Objective: turn the validated method into a paper-ready contribution.
Key results: submit a conference abstract, complete a parameter study across a defined set of 
conditions, draft a methods section.

**Late stage**, approaching thesis defense.
Objective: close remaining chapters and reach defense-ready status.
Key results: submit a chapter draft for committee review, incorporate feedback within a set 
turnaround, confirm a defense date.

### Worked example

```
Objective: Get the coupled model to a state where it can generate publishable results.

KR1: Core numerical method validated against an analytical case (target error < 5%)
KR2: Full model run across at least 3 representative conditions
KR3: First draft of methods section written

Mid-term confidence check:
  Status: at risk
  Why: KR1 took twice as long as expected, chasing down a conservation error

End of term:
  KR1 score: 0.8 (validated, error slightly above target, cause documented)
  KR2 score: 0.3 (ran 1 of 3 conditions, the KR1 debugging ate the term)
  KR3 score: 0.0 (not started)
  Reflection: the debugging detour was worth it and the fix should make the
  remaining runs faster, but it consumed the term.
  Carry forward: run the remaining 2 conditions, draft the methods section.
```

## Record-keeping through GitHub

We keep each student's OKR history in a private repository, one per student, so a student can see 
and edit only their own record. A student is added as a collaborator with write access rather 
than admin access, so they can open pull requests but cannot change repository settings.

Inside each repository, one file per term holds that term's Objective, Key Results, and the eventual 
end-of-term scoring, so a student's full multi-year record accumulates as a sequence of files with 
full git history behind it.

The review cycle maps onto pull requests directly. At term start, the student opens a pull request 
adding the new term's file with a draft Objective and Key Results. The supervisor reviews it as they 
would review code, pushes back inline on anything too vague or too safe, and merges once it reflects 
real agreement. At term end, the student opens a second pull request against the same file with their 
self-scores and reflection filled in, and the same review-and-merge pattern applies. Branch protection 
at the repository level requires supervisor approval before either pull request can merge, so nothing 
becomes final without a conversation happening first.

A template repository with the file structure and a short README makes spinning up a new student's 
repository fast, and it keeps every student's record following the same shape without extra effort 
each term.

## Adapting this elsewhere

None of this depends specifically on GitHub. Any version control system with pull or merge requests 
and per-repository or per-branch permissions would support the same workflow. What matters is the 
shape of the process, not the tool: a private, student-owned record, a lightweight review step built 
into how the record gets updated, and a fixed cadence that keeps the whole thing from either 
disappearing or turning into unreviewed busywork.
